entry.title: SAP Signavio Ocotber 2026 Product Release - Process Transformation Management and Process Governance
entry.content:
SAP Signavio October 2026 Product Release - Process Transformation Management

I'm excited to share the latest innovations for process transformation management and process governance as part of our SAP Signavio October 2026 product release!

Fresh off the SAP Transformation Excellence Summit in Berlin, where we explored how organizations can accelerate transformation and turn AI-powered insights into measurable business outcomes, this release brings several exciting innovations to help you do just that. From turning AI-generated recommendations into actionable transformation initiatives to tracking realized business value and continuously enriching initiatives with the latest insights, these enhancements help organizations move faster from insight to execution, keep transformation efforts on track, and demonstrate tangible business impact.

Let's take a closer look at what's new!

SAP Signavio Process Transformation Manager

Turn AI recommendations into action, track realized transformation value, and keep initiatives execution-ready.

Turn AI-powered recommendations into actionable transformation initiatives

Identifying process improvement opportunities is only the beginning. The real value comes from turning those insights into action. Transformation leads can now use the Process Consulting Agent to create actionable initiatives and supporting insights directly from AI-generated process optimization recommendations. When Process Consultaingn Agent identifies an improvement opportunity, your users can seamlessly turn the recommendation into structured transformation content while preserving the underlying process context, rationale, and supporting findings. This helps you bridge the gap between process analysis and execution planning without the need to manually recreate information. The same also extends to value management. Process Consulting Agent can use relevant findings from SAP Signavio Process Intelligence or user-provided business information to create structured manual value cases, helping teams connect identified improvement opportunities with expected business value. Key benefits include:

  • Accelerate insights to action: Turn AI-generated optimization recommendations into actionable transformation initiatives and insights with less manual effort.
  • Preserve valuable context: Keep supporting process findings, rationale, and recommendations connected to transformation work.
  • Streamline transformation planning: Create structured initiatives and insights directly from AI recommendations, reducing reliance on disconnected documents and manual processes.
  • Build on existing transformation work: Use existing transformation content as context to align new recommendations with ongoing initiatives and reduce duplication.
  • Connect process improvement to business value: Create manual value cases from Process Intelligence findings or user-provided inputs so improvement opportunities can be assessed and prioritized based on expected value.

Click here to watch the video demo for this feature

 

Keep transformation initiatives up to date with AI-assisted initiative enricher

Transformation doesn't stand still, and neither should your initiatives. As new process insights, business priorities, and improvement opportunities emerge, transformation teams need to continuously adapt their initiatives without duplicating work or starting from scratch.

With the new Initiative Enricher for AI-Assisted Transformation Advisory, transformation leads can enhance existing initiatives directly within SAP Signavio Process Transformation Manager. AI analyzes an initiative's existing insights, assets, and tasks, identifies where additional context could improve the recommendations, and proposes relevant new attributes, assets, and tasks. Suggested content is displayed alongside existing information, making it easy to identify what's new and avoid duplication. Importantly, you remain in full control. Every AI-generated suggestion can be individually reviewed and approved before adding to the initiative, ensuring you stay in control and understand where each recommendation comes from. Key benefits include:

  • Continuously strengthen initiatives: Enrich existing initiatives with relevant attributes, assets, and tasks without recreating work already in progress.
  • Identify opportunities for improvement: Receive AI-assisted guidance on missing information and additional context that could strengthen an initiative.
  • Avoid duplication: Compare proposed enhancements with existing initiative content before deciding what to add.
  • Maintain transparency and control: Review and selectively approve AI-generated suggestions, with clear visibility into their sources and attribution.

By making it easier to continuously enrich transformation work, this innovation helps you and your teams to keep initiatives relevant, actionable, and execution-ready as business needs evolve.

 

Track realized transformation value and demonstrate measurable business impact

Transformation success isn't just about identifying opportunities or estimating potential benefits. It's about demonstrating the value that has actually been achieved. With the latest value tracking and realization feature in SAP Signavio Process Transformation Manager, transformation leads can now capture, monitor, and visualize realized business value alongside expected value throughout the transformation lifecycle.

The capability supports both manually created value cases and value cases originating from SAP Signavio Process Intelligence, providing a more consistent approach to tracking business outcomes across transformation initiatives. Realized values can be entered manually or automatically synchronized from source systems where supported, giving teams the flexibility to track outcomes while maintaining transparency into the underlying data. New historical trend visualizations also make it easier to understand how realized value progresses over time, compare results against expected targets, and identify deviations that may require attention. Key benefits include:

  • Demonstrate measurable business impact: Track actual realized value alongside expected value to clearly distinguish planned benefits from achieved outcomes.
  • Enable end-to-end value tracking: Monitor business value from initial opportunity identification through execution to realized results across manual and system-sourced value cases.
  • Visualize value progression: Track historical value trends to understand progress toward targets, identify deviations, and support timely decisions.
  • Simplify value tracking and reporting: Automatically synchronize realized values from Process Insights and Process Intelligence when available, while enabling manual updates when needed.
  • Ensure data transparency and flexibility: Maintain source-system linkage and distinguish synchronized from manually adjusted values for more reliable reporting.
  • Strengthen transformation steering: Equip transformation teams and stakeholders with actionable insights to assess initiative performance, prioritize improvements, and demonstrate transformation success.

With this you can now move beyond measuring transformation potential to actually demonstrating tangible business results.

Click here to watch the video demo for this feature

 

Manage transformation tasks with greater flexibility and control

Successful transformation requires more than well-defined initiatives. It also depends on clear responsibilities, effective collaboration, and the ability to keep execution on track. The enhanced suite tasks experience introduces additional capabilities to help users manage transformation tasks more efficiently across SAP Signavio Process Transformation Suite. With new task attributes, including due dates, as well as enhanced filtering and sorting capabilities, users can better organize their work, identify priorities, and stay on top of upcoming deadlines. More granular access management also provides greater flexibility in controlling who can view or edit individual tasks, helping teams collaborate while maintaining appropriate permissions. Key benefits include:

  • Stay on top of priorities: Set task due dates and use enhanced filtering and sorting capabilities to organize work and manage deadlines.
  • Improve task visibility: Access additional task attributes for a clearer understanding of responsibilities and execution progress.
  • Gain greater control: Manage access at the individual task level with more granular permissions.
  • Support effective collaboration: Enable a more transparent, flexible, and scalable task management experience across transformation initiatives.

Click here and here to watch the video demos for this feature

Other Enhancements:

Beyond these innovations, the October release introduces further improvements to help transformation teams connect strategic objectives, process insights, and execution activities.

  • Visualize relationships between transformation initiatives and objectives: Gain a clearer understanding of how transformation initiatives contribute to strategic business goals with a new visual relationship graph in SAP Signavio Process Transformation Manager. By making connections between initiatives and their associated objectives visible, teams can more easily navigate transformation work, understand strategic alignment, and see how individual initiatives support broader transformation priorities.
  • Convert correction recommendations into transformation insights: Move more seamlessly from process analysis to transformation planning by converting data-driven correction recommendations from SAP Signavio Process Insights into structured insights in SAP Signavio Process Transformation Manager. This enhancement enables transformation leads to preserve important analytical findings and connect them to relevant transformation work, reducing manual effort while maintaining the context behind each recommendation.

 

Continue your transformation journey with SAP Signavio

You direct, AI executes. Realize value across your process transformation journey. The October 2026 release brings this vision to life, empowering organizations to accelerate transformation with AI while keeping people in control. From AI-powered recommendations to actionable initiatives and measurable business outcomes, SAP Signavio Process Transformation Manager helps teams move seamlessly from insight to execution and value realization.

entry.title: Re: Which APP can be used to mass update the credit limit...
entry.content:
Dear @xuqi_fangaf39f1,

I reviewed SAP KBA 3351046 and verified the available functionality in my tenant

To mass update credit limits for existing customers, you can use Schedule Credit Management Jobs (F3748) with the job template Update Credit Limit for Business Partners (SAP_FIN_UKM_MASSDATA_UPDATE_3)

 

Both the job template and the Credit Management Master Data API mentioned below require Advanced Credit Management (scope item 1QM), which requires an additional SAP S/4HANA Cloud license

The procedure is as follows:

  1. Open Schedule Credit Management Jobs (F3748)
  2. Create a new job and select Update Credit Limit for Business Partners
  3. Maintain the required selection criteria, such as Business Partner and Credit Segment
  4. Select Test Run to check the results before updating the data
  5. Select Update Run and schedule the job when you are ready to apply the changes

IMPORTANT: According to SAP KBA 3351046 this job performs a mass re-evaluation of credit limits based on the configured credit limit calculation rules. It does not directly assign different manually specified credit limit amounts to individual customers.

If the requirement is to update existing customers with specific credit limit amounts, SAP also provides the Credit Management Master Data API (API_CRDTMBUSINESSPARTNER_0001)

This API supports updating existing credit limits through the PATCH operation and can be used for mass updates through an integration

More details below:

SAP KBA 3351046 – Update Credit Limit of Business Partner

SAP Help – Update Credit Limit for Business Partners

Best Regards,

Dawid

entry.title: SAP Signavio Process and Journey Modeling: what's new in the October 2026 release

The October 2026 release of SAP Signavio Process Modeler marks a significant step in how you model, govern, and connect process knowledge across the enterprise. At the center is a completely reimagined Process Modeler canvas, built from the ground up with a modern, AI-native modeling experience and deep integration with the SAP Signavio Process Transformation Suite. Alongside it, this release broadens AI access, strengthens process landscape visibility, and lays the structural foundation for your transformation initiatives.  

From making AI-assisted modeling available as a Base AI capability, a beta MCP server for AI agents, and the stage one release of the Process Atom Central Repository, this release advances both the day-to-day experience of process professionals and the longer-term vision of an intelligent, interconnected process landscape. A new Process Governance Dashboard rounds out the release, giving administrators a consolidated view of workspace health, without manual audits. 

Here is a summary of what the new October release brings to you: 

The new SAP Signavio Process Modeler canvas 

Starting now, the new SAP Signavio Process Modeler canvas is available to all customers, bringing a completely reimagined modeling experience designed for the next generation of process transformation.  

It was built from the ground up around three core ideas:  

  • A modern, intuitive modeling experience that helps users focus on process improvement rather than tooling 
  • Embedded AI-native modeling experience where built-in intelligence guides you from the first element to a ready-to-use process model 
  • Deep integration with the SAP Signavio Process Transformation Suite, connecting process design with governance, collaboration, and insights for a more actionable view of transformation

Read the full story in our dedicated blog post.

 

AI-assisted Process Modeler Now Included in Base AI 

Effective October 5th 2026, AI-assisted Process Modeler moves from a Premium AI feature to a Base AI capability for all SAP Signavio Process Modeler customers. No AI units required, no activation through SAP for Me. Workspace administrators can enable it directly within SAP Signavio AI Services settings, making it easier than ever to roll out AI-enabled process modeling across the organization. 

For teams already using the feature, nothing changes in how it works: usage simply no longer consumes AI units. For those exploring it for the first time, AI-assisted Process Modeler lets your users generate process diagrams from text descriptions, images, and tables in just a few clicks, reducing modeling effort and making process documentation more accessible to a broader range of contributors. A fair usage limit is expected to apply at the workspace level. 

 

Find out how to activate AI capabilities in your workspace and assign users in this SAP Help Portal post. 

 

Turn your process data into a knowledge source for any AI agent with the SAP Signavio MCP Server (Beta) 

Equip AI agents to answer natural language questions about your processes, build custom use cases on top of your process information, and accelerate AI-driven transformation, all through a standardized MCP (Model Context Protocol) connector that works with the AI tools your teams already use. No custom development. No dedicated connectors. 

Want to learn how to get started with the SAP Signavio MCP server? You can find the step-by-step in our dedicated guide here.  

 

Stage One Release of Process Atom Central Repository 

Process knowledge today is fragmented. Defined in one place, rediscovered in another, and often lost along the way. The Process Atom Central Repository changes that by establishing a single, governed home for Process Atoms: reusable units of process behavior that teams and AI agents can build on together. 

This Stage One Release delivers the foundational layer, introducing the Process Atom as a structured, entitled object with a central browsable repository and a basic publishing lifecycle. It focuses on establishing the core building block on which governance, AI-assisted authoring, and broader suite capabilities will follow.

entry.title: Introducing the new SAP Signavio Process Modeler canvas
entry.content:
For years, process modeling has been the foundation of business process transformation. Organizations documented how work gets done, captured expertise, and built repositories of process knowledge. But the world has changed. 

Today, companies face constant disruption. Market conditions shift faster than ever; customer expectations continue to rise, and AI is redefining how organizations operate. In this environment, transformation is no longer a one-time initiative. It is a continuous capability. 

To meet this challenge, process modeling itself must evolve. 

That is why we are excited to announce the General Availability of the new SAP Signavio Process Modeler canvas. 

 

Starting now, the new canvas is available to all customers, bringing a completely reimagined modeling experience designed for the next generation of process transformation. Built from the ground up, it combines an intuitive user experience, embedded AI capabilities, and deep integration across SAP Signavio Process Transformation Suite.  

Why we rebuilt process modeling and how it’ll support you 

Traditional process modeling tools were designed primarily for documentation. They helped organizations visualize and standardize processes but often required significant expertise and effort to create and maintain models. 

As transformation accelerated, organizations needed more than documentation. They needed tools that help teams collaborate, adapt faster, and connect process design to real business outcomes. 

The new SAP Signavio Process Modeler canvas was created to address this shift. 

Rather than simply updating an existing application, we reimagined the experience around three core principles: 

Effortless by design 

Modeling should feel natural, not complex. 

The new canvas introduces a modern modeling engine, redesigned BPMN shapes, real-time collaboration capabilities, improved navigation, and a streamlined user experience that helps users focus on process improvement rather than tooling. Whether you're an experienced process analyst or a first-time contributor, creating and maintaining process models becomes faster and more intuitive. 

Intelligent by default 

No one should have to start from a blank canvas. 

Embedded AI capabilities help accelerate modeling by generating process diagrams from text, providing intelligent suggestions, and assisting users throughout the modeling journey. As organizations increasingly adopt AI-powered ways of working, process modeling can now move from manual creation toward intelligent assistance and, ultimately, autonomous evolution.  

Natively connected 

Processes create the most value when they are part of a larger transformation ecosystem. 

The new canvas is deeply integrated with the SAP Signavio Process Transformation Suite, connecting process design with governance, collaboration, transformation initiatives, and process insights. This creates a more connected and actionable view of transformation, enabling you to move seamlessly from designing processes to improving them.  

What's available 

The GA release introduces a range of features that make process modeling more collaborative, intelligent, and connected: 

  • Modern cloud-native modeling canvas 
  • Real-time collaborative editing 
  • Enhanced BPMN experience and shape management 
  • AI-assisted modeling capabilities, including text-to-process  
  • Intelligent auto-suggestions and process generation support 
  • Integrated navigation across SAP Signavio applications 
  • Improved repository and attribute management 
  • Lifecycle management capabilities and governance controls 
  • Deep connectivity across the SAP Signavio portfolio, such as with SAP Signavio Process Transformation Suite and SAP Signavio Process Intelligence 

Together, these capabilities help organizations reduce modeling effort, improve consistency, accelerate adoption, and create greater business value from their process investments. 

New canvas innovations 

The following capabilities are available exclusively on the new SAP Signavio Process Modeler canvas. They represent a new generation of modeling experiences, built from the ground up to reduce effort, accelerate collaboration, and bring intelligence directly into the modeling workflow. Organizations that activate the new canvas will have immediate access to these innovations as part of the GA release. 

  • Inline Suggestion - the canvas anticipates your next move. As you build, Inline Suggestion delivers real-time, context-aware completions directly within the canvas, drawing on what you have already modeled to suggest the most logical next steps. You spend less time searching and more time shaping processes that reflect how work actually flows.

     

  • Auto Completion - no more starting from scratch. Auto Completion analyzes your current canvas and generates complete, contextually relevant suggestions for what should come next. It closes the gap between a partial model and a finished one, accelerating first drafts, reducing inconsistencies, and helping teams reach a working process faster. 

     

  •  Modeling Shapes Personalization - your toolkit, built around the way you work. A redesigned, personalized shapes toolbar puts a curated set of new BPMN shapes, icons, and visual elements at your fingertips, making it faster to find, apply, and organize the building blocks your models rely on. New visual experiences across the toolbar help modelers work with greater speed and consistency, without the friction of searching through what they do not need. 

     

  • Real-time Collaboration - process design is rarely a solo activity. Real-time Collaboration brings teams into a shared modeling workspace simultaneously, enabling live co-editing, in-context feedback, and cross-functional alignment without file handoffs or version conflicts. Whether teams are co-located or distributed, everyone can contribute to process design when it matters, keeping transformation moving at the pace business demands. 

Auto Layout - a well-structured model communicates more. Auto Layout automatically arranges your process diagram into a clean, logical structure, eliminating the manual effort of formatting and repositioning elements by hand. With a single action, you focus on process content rather than visual presentation, accelerating the path from model to business value. 

 

 

A new era of process transformation 

The evolution of process modeling mirrors the evolution of business transformation itself. 

Organizations first documented processes. Then they began analyzing and improving them. Now they must continuously adapt and transform. 

The new SAP Signavio Process Modeler canvas is built for this next chapter. It empowers organizations to move beyond static process diagrams and toward living process ecosystems that support ongoing change and continuous improvement.  

Available now 

Following successful alpha and beta programs with customers and early adopters, the new SAP Signavio Process Modeler canvas is now generally available and open to all customers. Organizations can begin leveraging the new experience to model faster, collaborate more effectively, and accelerate their transformation journeys.  

Process modeling has always been the starting point of transformation. With the new SAP Signavio Process Modeler canvas, it becomes an accelerator for what's next.

Administrators must explicitly activate the capability, assign user groups, and turn on navigation visibility before anyone can see or use it. This gives workspace admins full control over the rollout timeline and training readiness. Download the activation handbook for the full setup process.

Hi @AIDream ,

The error message in your Monitor Value Chains screenshot identifies the relevant issue: “Error in external tax system: SOAP:1032 SRT: Wrong Content-Type and empty HTTP-Body received…”

The NBIC purchase order has been processed successfully, but the subsequent IC Sales Order (SOIC) creation fails when the system encounters an external tax calculation communication error.

This matches the symptom documented in SAP KBA 3148132 Error in external tax system: SOAP:1032 SRT: Wrong Content-Type and empty (SAP_COM_0177) for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition.

entry.title: Re: Questions regarding 5HP + 5W2
entry.content:
Hi @AIDream ,

Your proposed combination of 5HP Advanced Intercompany Stock Transfer and 5W2 Group Valuation is aligned with SAP's documented approach.

SAP Note 3100892 recommends using 5HP, 5D2 and 5MQ with 5W2, together with the required expert configuration, to enable intercompany profit elimination in inventory accounting.

SAP Note 3093830 confirms that intercompany margin elimination is supported for the advanced intercompany processes 5HP and 5D2.

1. Different price controls (S/V) between plants

S and V are price control indicators, not valuation classes.

Price control is maintained at valuation-area level, so different plants can generally use different price controls for the same material.

SAP Note 3093830 (version 33) does not list a restriction prohibiting the proposed S/V combinations for RM12 and FG126. However, it does not explicitly validate their complete group valuation accounting behavior either.

For production of FG126 in Plant 1710, two additional restrictions in the same note are relevant:

  • Period-end based production accounting (BEI) is not enabled with group valuation. SAP recommends event-based production accounting (3F0) where the production scenario is supported by 3F0.

  • Order plan costs are not calculated for the group valuation view in make-to-stock scenarios. SAP directs users to the leading ledger for plan costs.

2. Returns - SAP Note 3192546

SAP Note 3192546 states that customer return processes referencing Advanced Intercompany Stock Transfer are not supported and instructs users to use an intercompany stock transfer return.

However, 2TS - Intercompany Stock Transfer Returns is incompatible with 5W2, as confirmed by SAP Note 3093830 and KBA 3398511.

SAP KBA 3608818 recommends considering 5HP when 1P9 or 2TS is required but 5W2 is already included.

This recommendation does not describe the actual return document flow or establish that a reverse-direction STO is supported with 5HP + 5W2.

SAP Note 3192546 also identifies intercompany invoice corrections as an unsupported scenario.

Therefore, the supported return procedure, including document references and accounting treatment, requires clarification with SAP before implementation. I would not assume that reversing the STO direction is sufficient.

3. Group valuation price with multiple supplying plants

According to SAP Help (Group Costing in Inventory Accounting), ledger 4G can be used in Inventory Accounting to calculate standard prices from the group valuation perspective.

The group cost estimate rolls up the cost component structure across production steps, with costs shown separately by supplying company code, including the relevant profit markup. SAP documents valuation variant 4GL in the configuration activity Define Valuation Variants per Plant for group cost estimates.

SAP Note 3093830 confirms that intercompany margin elimination is supported for 5HP.

However, this does not establish how the group valuation price for FG126 in Plant 1010 is determined when the material is supplied by both Plants 1710 and 1310.

In particular, the cited documentation does not confirm whether a group cost estimate combines multiple supplying plants or how receipts from different internal suppliers affect the group valuation price.

SAP Note 3192546 also states that intercompany profit (markup) as part of the Material Ledger and actual costing cost component view is not supported. This restriction should be distinguished from the group costing information described above and from intercompany margin elimination supported for 5HP.

For your scenario, I recommend reviewing the group cost estimate of FG126 in Plant 1010 and the corresponding ledger 4G postings for receipts from Plants 1710 and 1310.

I would not assume that the latest receipt price is adopted or that an automatic weighted-average calculation across supplying plants is performed without verifying the applicable valuation settings.

4. Purchasing view for FG126

If FG126 uses material type FERT, SAP Support has documented that the Purchasing view can be enabled through SSCUI 103539 Define Attributes of Material Types.

Select FERT, enable Purchasing under User Departments, and save the configuration.

The required purchasing data can then be maintained for FG126 in Plant 1010. A separate material type is not required solely to enable this view.

Additional consideration

SAP KBA 3398511 confirms that mutually exclusive scope items cannot be changed after deployment without system reprovisioning. The decision to activate 5W2 should therefore be finalized during initial scoping.

SAP references

    • SAP Note 3093830 - SAP S/4HANA Cloud: Release Restriction Note for Group Valuation
    • SAP Note 3100892 -Group Valuation in SAP S/4HANA Cloud
    • SAP KBA 3398511 - Activation of Scope Item 5W2 (Group Valuation) in SAP Central Business Configuration: Dependencies & Restrictions
    • SAP Note 3192546 - SAP S/4HANA Cloud: Restrictions and General Information for Advanced Intercompany Stock Transfer
    • SAP KBA 3608818 - What is the alternative solution for scope items 1P9 and 2TS if scope item 5W2 has been included?

    • SAP Help - Group Valuation (5W2), SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition
    • SAP Learning - Using Special Procurement Types
    • SAP Community - How to activate the Purchasing view for material type in SAP S/4HANA Cloud

Elena P.

entry.title: Re: How to create regular OR-type sales orders with refer...
entry.content:
Hi @xuqi_fangaf39f1 ,

Based on your description, your requirement is to retain the Sales Scheduling Agreement for long-term customer forecasts while creating separate OR sales orders for confirmed customer demand.

The objective is to ensure that confirmed OR quantities replace the corresponding forecast requirements in MRP, rather than creating duplicate demand.

1. OR sales orders with reference to Sales Scheduling Agreements

I could not identify a documented standard function in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition that creates an OR sales order with reference to a sales scheduling agreement and automatically consumes its forecast requirements.

It is important to distinguish document copy control from MRP requirements consumption. Even if a document reference were available, this would not necessarily implement the forecast offset logic.

2. Recommended standard functionality to evaluate: Planning Delivery Schedule

SAP provides a Planning Delivery Schedule as part of the Sales Scheduling Agreement process.

This is an internal schedule that can be generated from the customer Forecast Delivery Schedule and used to adjust requirements planning.

When relevant for MRP, the Planning Delivery Schedule replaces the Forecast Delivery Schedule for requirements planning, while the original customer forecast remains unchanged.

For your scenario, I would evaluate the following process:

  • Retain the original customer forecast in the Forecast Delivery Schedule.

  • Generate a Planning Delivery Schedule for MRP-relevant requirements.

  • Create standard OR sales orders for confirmed customer quantities.

  • Adjust the corresponding Planning Delivery Schedule quantities to account for demand already represented by OR orders.

For example, if the customer forecast is 1,000 units and 300 units are confirmed through an OR order, the intended planning result would be:

  • Original Forecast Delivery Schedule: 1,000 units, unchanged.

  • Planning Delivery Schedule: 700 units.

  • OR sales order: 300 units.

  • Total MRP demand: 1,000 units rather than 1,300.

This is a proposed process design, not automatic OR consumption provided by the Planning Delivery Schedule.

Important: When a Planning Delivery Schedule is regenerated from updated customer forecasts, existing schedule lines may be overwritten. Therefore, any OR-related adjustments must be reconciled and reapplied as necessary.

3. Extensibility if automatic synchronization is required

If manual adjustments are not practical, a side-by-side extension could be investigated to synchronize confirmed OR quantities with the internal Planning Delivery Schedule.

However, the supported interfaces must be verified before selecting an architecture.

SAP explicitly documents that the Sales Scheduling Agreement (A2X) API, API_SALES_SCHEDULING_AGREEMENT, supports only GET operations for delivery schedules and schedule lines. Its constraints exclude creating, updating, or deleting these entities.

Therefore, this API cannot be used directly to update the Planning Delivery Schedule quantities.

This does not rule out every extensibility option, but a supported write interface for the required operation would need to be identified and validated with SAP.

A proof of concept should cover order changes, cancellations, partial quantities, updated customer forecast releases, and Planning Delivery Schedule regeneration.

4. Alternatives if the process can change

  • JIT delivery schedules: If confirmed customer requirements can be processed within the same sales scheduling agreement, the JIT delivery schedule takes precedence over the forecast within the applicable JIT horizon. This avoids overlapping forecast and firm releases but does not create separate OR sales orders.

  • Planned Independent Requirements with strategy 40 (Planning with Final Assembly): Forecast demand is maintained as PIRs and consumed by sales order requirements according to the configured consumption settings. This supports OR sales orders but requires changing the forecast planning design rather than consuming MRP-relevant scheduling agreement requirements directly.

Recommendation

If both document types are mandatory, I would first evaluate the standard Planning Delivery Schedule functionality in scope item 3NR, including its MRP relevance, manual maintenance, and regeneration behavior.

This is closer to your existing process because the original customer forecast can remain unchanged while internal planning requirements are managed separately.

However, automatic synchronization between OR sales orders and the Planning Delivery Schedule is not established as standard functionality. If automation is essential, its technical feasibility should be confirmed before committing to an extensibility solution.

SAP references

  • SAP Help - Sales Scheduling Agreements

  • SAP Best Practices 3NR - Maintain Planning Delivery Schedule Instruction

  • SAP Best Practices 3NR - Generate Planning Delivery Schedule

  • SAP Help - Change Sales Scheduling Agreements (VA32)

  • SAP Help - Sales Scheduling Agreement (A2X) API

  • SAP Help - Business Add-Ins for Sales Scheduling Agreements

Best regards, 
Elena P.

entry.title: Re: How to perform credit approval for blocked outbound d...
entry.content:
Hi @xuqi_fangaf39f1 ,

For SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition 2608, the relevant application for processing credit-blocked outbound deliveries is Manage Documented Credit Decisions (F5587A), the successor to the deprecated application F5587.

SAP explicitly documents the new application and its activation requirements. The behavior you describe may be related to the transition to the new Documented Credit Decision (DCD) functionality.

1. Check whether the new DCD functionality is activated

SAP KBA 3788656 addresses the situation where Manage Documented Credit Decisions (F5587A) is not available after the 2608 upgrade.

The new application requires the feature Rebuild of Documented Credit Decision (FIN_FSCM_REBUILD_DCD).

Before activating this feature, please follow the official SAP Help procedure Switching from the Deprecated Version to the New Version of the Manage Documented Credit Decisions App.

The procedure includes mandatory data migration, workflow-event reprocessing, feature activation, and authorization steps. The migration changes the underlying DCD business object and cannot be reversed.

If your system was not previously using the deprecated F5587 application, SAP provides a separate procedure, Steps for Configuring Documented Credit Decisions.

2. Verify the new application and business catalog

SAP KBA 3747588 confirms that the new business catalog SAP_FIN_BC_CR_DCD_PC may not be visible until the feature is activated.

After completing the activation procedure, verify the catalog and assign the required application authorizations to the credit controller role.

SAP documents these IAM apps:

  • F5587A_TRAN Manage Documented Credit Decision

  • F5587A_02_TRAN Edit Documented Credit Decision

  • F5587A_03_TRAN Display Documented Credit Decision

The standard business role is SAP_BR_CREDIT_CONTROLLER.

3. Use the correct action for the blocked delivery

In Manage Documented Credit Decisions (F5587A), SAP distinguishes between:

  • Recheck perform another credit check.

  • Release release the credit-blocked SD document.

  • Approve approve the current step in a configured approval process.

Therefore, an inactive Approve button in Manage Credit Cases does not establish whether the blocked outbound delivery can be released.

Please check the corresponding DCD in F5587A and use Release or Recheck, as appropriate for the document status and your authorization.

If approval hierarchies are configured, also verify the responsible approver and the relevant rules in Manage Credit Management Rules.

Recommendation

I would first check whether FIN_FSCM_REBUILD_DCD has been activated and whether the new F5587A application and catalog are available.

If not, follow the official SAP migration or initial configuration procedure before attempting to release the blocked delivery.

If F5587A is already available but Release remains disabled, the next step is to examine the specific DCD status, approval process, and user authorizations.

SAP references

  • SAP Help - Switching from the Deprecated Version to the New Version of Manage Documented Credit Decisions

  • SAP Help - Performing Mass Activities (Release, Recheck, Approve)

  • SAP KBA 3788656 - Manage Documented Credit Decision (F5587A) not available after 2608

  • SAP KBA 3747588 - Business catalog SAP_FIN_BC_CR_DCD_PC not available

  • SAP KBA 3715354 - Activation of feature for Manage Documented Credit Decisions (New Version)

entry.title: What's New in SAP Subscription Billing (Q3 2026)
entry.content:
This edition of our quarterly series highlighting the latest improvements in SAP Subscription Billing covers a range of updates, from flexible subscription onboarding and smarter pricing logic to enhanced data privacy controls and more granular billing configuration. Read on to see what's new and how these changes can benefit your business.

 

Phased Subscription Onboarding with Subscription Ramps

Bringing new customers onto a subscription often works better when conditions are introduced gradually — lower prices or reduced quantities at the start, stepping up over time as the customer realizes full value. Subscription ramps make this possible by letting you define successive phases within a subscription, each with its own conditions, as agreed in a ramp deal.

Each ramp period can specify a different combination of:

  • Product
  • Product price (via rate plan or customized prices and discounts)
  • Product quantity (via subscription parameters for license-based subscriptions)

Ramp periods are stored as snapshots. The item list in the Manage Subscriptions app has been redesigned to give you a clear overview of all snapshots at a glance, without needing to switch views.

 

The fields displayed in the item list depend on the ramp profile configured in the Manage Business Configuration app under Subscription Settings:

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

You can create up to 10 ramp periods per subscription. Ramp periods are always adjacent to each other without gaps or overlaps. Once the last ramp period ends, its conditions remain in effect until a new snapshot is created.

Key capabilities
  • Create ramp periods during subscription creation or while the subscription is in a pending state
  • Adjust the length of ramp periods (pending subscriptions only)
  • Edit ramp period content in effective subscriptions, including splitting a period to apply different conditions for part of it
  • Delete individual or all ramp periods while the subscription is pending
Example

A rolling subscription for a printer has two initial 6-month ramp periods with decreasing discounts on the price per copy. The third ramp period defines the longer-term conditions with no discount. After the last ramp period ends, those conditions remain valid.

 

For full details, see Subscription Ramps.

 

Bill Consolidation Control at Subscription Level

You can now configure bill splitting directly in billing profiles using the new Split Bills by Subscription setting in the Manage Business Configuration app. When this setting is active, each subscription produces its own bill. Charges from different subscriptions are never merged, even when other aggregation criteria would normally combine them.

 

The setting is also visible in the Manage Billing Data app on the General Info tab of the billing profile:

 

This is particularly useful when customers require itemized billing per subscription for internal cost allocation, auditing, or contractual reasons.

Example

A corporate customer has multiple active subscriptions for different departments. With Split Bills by Subscription enabled, each department receives a separate bill for its own subscription, simplifying internal chargebacks.

 

Working Directly with Amounts in Pricing Logic

Pricing logic can now handle monetary amounts natively. You can calculate amounts, use them in conditional logic, and return them as price elements, all within a single price element specification. A new amount field type is available in the Manage Field Catalog app. Amount fields can be included in lookup tables and either returned directly as a price or passed on as a property to subsequent components in the pricing tree.

Three new pricing tree components support this:

  • Amount Calculation: Calculates an amount based on a price condition.
  • Amount Comparison: Compares two monetary amount fields (or one against the reference price property) and branches logic based on the result.
  • Set Price Element: Returns an amount field as a price element.

There are three new components you can use to calculate amounts and build pricing logic based on them:

  • Operator: Amount Calculation
    This component is used to calculate an amount which you can then use in subsequent steps of the pricing tree.
  • Comparator: Amount Comparison
    This component compares the values of a monetary amount field to another one, or to the reference price property. It decides on different action paths depending on the result.
  • Function: Set Price Element
    This component is the pricing tree component used to generate a price element by returning an amount field.

Amount fields can be defined as output fields in lookup tables, making them accessible via the Table Lookup component. Furthermore, amount fields can be used within the Execute Formula component for further calculation before returning a price element.

Results, including amount fields, are visible in the Analyze Pricing Documents app.

Example

A pricing rule applies a flat monthly fee stored in a lookup table, adjusted by a multiplier based on the customer's contracted tier. The Amount Calculation component handles the multiplication, and Set Price Element returns the result directly as a charge.

To find out more, see Pricing Tree.

 

Volume-Based Discounts on Usage Events and Transactions

You can now define prices based on the number of usage events or transactions, represented by the count of usage records. The standard fields cumulativeUsageCount and usageCount are now available for this purpose in your pricing configuration.

During usage rating, the number of usage records is determined and passed to the billing process. In the Manage Billing Data app, the consumed usage record count is displayed in the new Usage Count field. If cross-billing cycle aggregation is in use, a second Usage Count field is shown for the aggregated value.

Example

A bike rental provider wants to apply a volume discount only when customers meet two thresholds within a billing cycle:

  • Monthly ride count: The number of individual rides taken (usage record count)
  • Monthly spend threshold: The total value of those rides (aggregated quantity)

The discount is applied only when both thresholds are met. Using usageCount for the ride count and cumulativeUsageCount for the aggregated spend across billing cycles, the provider can configure a two-dimensional pricing rule. The resulting discount is calculated during usage rating and is visible to the customer on their bill.

 

Data Retention and Deletion Policies per Legal Entity

Managing data privacy across multiple legal entities within a single SAP Subscription Billing tenant is now more precise. You can configure data retention rules per company code, using SAP Subscription Billing's integration with the next-generation SAP Data Privacy Integration service.

What this enables
  • Define multiple business purposes within the same tenant, for example, separate purposes for individual customers and corporate customers per company.

  • Configure retention rules per combination of data controller (company code), data subject role (individual customer or corporate customer), and information lifecycle management object type (customer, subscription, or bill), with separate residence and retention periods for each object type.

  • Use company code as the anchor for data protection processes, ensuring deletion and retention are applied per legal entity.

To include customers and business documents in deletion processes, a company code must be maintained on all relevant records.

In the Manage Business Configuration app, company mapping is now configurable on the Markets tab:

 
Example

A subscription business operating in both Germany and the United States needs to apply different retention periods for customer data in each jurisdiction. With company code-based retention rules, each legal entity's data is governed independently within the same tenant.

For full details on data protection in SAP Subscription Billing, see Data Protection and Privacy.

 

Billing in Advance Configurable Directly in Subscriptions

Managing recurring charges that are billed both in advance and in arrears previously required separate rate plans for each combination. You can now reduce that overhead by enabling users to set the Billing in Advance option directly at the subscription item level. To enable this, define the Billing in Advance setting as a parameter in a rate plan template. In any subscription item using a rate plan based on that template, users can then override the default value, choosing advance or arrears billing as needed, without requiring a separate rate plan.

The setting appears on the item-level Billing tab in the Manage Subscriptions app, using the parameter label defined in the rate plan template.

Example

A company offers a software subscription that is typically billed in arrears, but certain enterprise customers prefer billing in advance for budget planning purposes. Rather than maintaining two separate rate plans, the subscription manager simply sets the billing preference at the subscription item level.

 

Pricing Configuration Apps Now Available in SAP Build Work Zone

A quick but useful update: the pricing configuration apps are now accessible in the SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition interface. For more information, see Integration with SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition.

 

This wraps up the Q3 2026 update for SAP Subscription Billing. As always, the goal behind these features is to give you more flexibility and control, whether that's in how you onboard customers, structure your pricing, or manage compliance across entities.
We'll be back at the end of Q4 with an overview of the latest features. Until then, keep innovating!

_____________________________________________________________

Subscribe to Never Miss New Features

To get notified about future update blogs, subscribe to SAP Subscription Billing in the SAP Community:


 

 

 

We also encourage you to subscribe to our What's New page on SAP Help Portal for a full list of updates:

entry.title: From Datasphere to SAC: When a Model Becomes a Business Answer
entry.content:
After working through the BW-to-Datasphere and S/4HANA-to-Datasphere sides of an analytics project, I started looking at the final part of the landscape a little differently.

We had spent time understanding the existing reporting logic, bringing data into Datasphere, building the required views, defining measures, and organizing the data into analytical models. Eventually, all that work had to reach SAP Analytics Cloud. This is where things get interesting.

A model can be activated successfully. The measures can return the expected values. The joins can work as intended. You can open the model, run your queries, and convince yourself that the development is moving in the right direction.

Then you build the SAC story.

A KPI shows an unexpected number. A filter changes the result in a way you didn't anticipate. A chart works in one context but behaves differently when the same data is consumed somewhere else. And suddenly, the problem doesn't look like a modeling problem anymore.

At least, not at first.

During my work with Datasphere and SAC, I started realizing that the last part of the analytics landscape deserves just as much attention as everything that happens before it. Because building a model and making that model useful to the business are two very different things.

The model was ready. Was the reporting ready?

In one of our project scenarios, we were working with financial and sales reporting requirements that needed to be exposed through SAC.

The Datasphere side involved the usual layers: raw data, harmonization views, reporting views, and analytical models. On the SAC side, the requirement was to turn those models into something business users could actually work with.

We were not building a single chart and calling it done.

The story needed to support different perspectives of the business: an executive overview, regional performance, customer analysis, and finance. That meant dealing with KPIs, charts, tables, filters, and different levels of detail. The obvious approach would have been to finish the Datasphere models first and then start building the story.

But I found that the relationship between the two is more iterative than that.

While building the SAC story, questions started coming up that were not obvious when looking at the model in isolation.

Does this measure represent the number the business expects to see?
Should this filter affect every widget on the page?
Should this calculation be reusable across multiple stories, or does it only make sense in one particular visualization?
Does the user need the aggregated number, or do they need to understand what is contributing to it?

These questions influence the modeling decisions just as much as they influence the story design, and that is where I started seeing SAC as more than the final presentation layer. It becomes the place where the quality of the entire analytical design is tested.

A KPI is a small number with a lot of responsibility

One thing I have come to appreciate is how much responsibility we place on a KPI card.

A chart gives the user some context. A table lets them inspect the underlying values. But a KPI often presents a single number and expects the user to trust it immediately.

Imagine an executive opening a sales dashboard.

The first thing they see is total sales. Below that, they see regional performance, customer contribution, and a breakdown of financial metrics. If the total is incorrect, the entire dashboard loses credibility. But the interesting part is that the number can be wrong for several different reasons.

The source data may be incomplete. The Datasphere model may aggregate the data differently than expected. A filter may be applied incorrectly. A measure may have the wrong semantic definition. Or the SAC widget may be consuming a different model or connection than the developer assumes.

From the user's perspective, all of these problems look the same. 

The dashboard is showing the wrong number.

From the developer's perspective, they are completely different problems. This is why I prefer to validate a KPI at the model level before spending time polishing its appearance in SAC. If the analytical model returns the wrong result, changing the formatting, chart type, or story layout will not solve the underlying problem. And if the model returns the correct result but the SAC widget does not, the investigation needs to move toward the consumption layer.

The important thing is to identify where the result changes, rather than assuming that the layer where the problem becomes visible is the layer where it originated.

Filters are where a simple dashboard can become complicated

Another part of SAC development that deserves more attention is filter behavior.

In our reporting work, the story needed to support filters such as Year, Period, Region, Product Group, Sales Organization, and GL Account.

Individually, these are straightforward requirements. The complexity appears when they start interacting with different charts, tables, and KPIs.

Consider a user selecting a particular region. They expect the sales KPI, regional chart, customer table, and other relevant widgets to reflect that selection consistently.

But not every widget necessarily uses the same model or has the same dimensional context.

A filter that makes sense for one model may not be available in another. Two models may represent the same business concept differently. A dimension may be present in one analytical model but absent from another.

This is where a dashboard that looks correct during development can become confusing for the user. The issue is not necessarily that the filter is broken. It may be that the underlying models do not support the same interpretation of that filter. For me, this reinforced the importance of thinking about filters while designing the Datasphere models, not just when configuring the SAC story.

Before adding a global filter, I would want to understand which models it needs to affect, whether the relevant dimensions are aligned, and what the expected behavior should be for every widget.

A filter is not simply a control on the screen. It represents a business expectation about how the data should respond.

Then there is the question of where a calculation belongs

This connects directly to the first article in this series, where I discussed translating existing BW reporting logic into Datasphere.

During that work, one question kept coming back: should a particular calculation live in Datasphere or in SAC?

I think this becomes much easier to answer when we stop looking at the calculation itself and start looking at how it will be used. 

Suppose we have a financial measure that needs a particular sign convention.

If that convention represents a reusable business rule, implementing it in the appropriate Datasphere modeling layer can make the result consistent for multiple consumers.

If we instead reproduce the same calculation independently in several SAC stories, we introduce more places where the logic can diverge.

Now consider a calculation that exists purely to support a particular chart or a presentation-specific comparison. That may be better handled in SAC, depending on the requirement and the capabilities involved. 

The point is not that every calculation belongs in Datasphere. It is that we should know why a calculation exists before deciding where to implement it.

I have found this question useful:

If another report needs the same business result tomorrow, should it have to recreate this logic?

If the answer is no, that is a good reason to investigate whether the logic belongs in a reusable model.

This decision affects maintainability, consistency, and how much work is required when the reporting requirement changes.

When a working SAC story is not the end of the story

One of the more interesting issues I encountered was outside the normal SAC story development process.

We were exploring the use of SAC KPI tiles in SAP Build Work Zone. The requirement was to make analytical information available through the Work Zone experience, rather than requiring users to navigate into the SAC story every time they wanted to see a KPI.

The important detail was that the SAC story was using a live connection to a Datasphere analytical model. The story itself could load the Datasphere data correctly.

However, when the same type of KPI was consumed through a Work Zone tile, the request failed with a FAILED_TO_FETCH_DATA error. What made this particularly interesting was that the behavior differed depending on the model type.

KPI tiles using SAC-based acquired models worked, while the equivalent approach using live Datasphere models did not behave the same way.

At that point, it would have been easy to keep changing the Datasphere model or rebuilding the SAC chart. But the fact that the story itself could retrieve the data suggested that we needed to investigate the consumption path as well. The question was no longer simply whether the model worked. It was whether the model and its live connection were supported in the context in which we were trying to consume them.

We investigated the data-fetching path and the relevant connection behavior, and the issue also raised questions about the limitations of the integration between the two environments. I wouldn't describe this as a solved problem. The important lesson was what it revealed about the architecture.

A model working in SAC does not automatically mean every way of embedding or consuming that model will work.

That distinction matters when designing analytics for more than one entry point.

A story, a KPI tile, and an embedded analytical experience may all appear to be displaying the same information, but they can involve different consumption mechanisms and constraints.

Those differences need to be considered during solution design, not discovered after the dashboard has already been built.

Sometimes the problem is not the model or the story. It is the environment.

The Work Zone investigation also connected to another challenge we were dealing with: the SAC and Datasphere tenants were operating in different regions.

The Datasphere tenant was in US21, while the SAC tenant was in US20.

This became relevant when investigating the proposed live connectivity approach. It introduced a dependency that could not be resolved simply by changing a measure or adjusting a chart. The model could be valid. The story could be valid. Yet the intended integration still depended on the connection architecture and the constraints of the environments involved.

We had to consider the tenant setup and discuss the approach internally and with the client while working through the support guidance.

This was a useful reminder that analytics architecture does not stop at the boundary of a Datasphere space or an SAC story. The connection between those environments is part of the solution too. I think this is particularly important when planning live analytics, embedded scenarios, and integrations across multiple SAP services.

Before committing to an approach, I would want to validate the actual connectivity path and the intended consumption scenario, not just confirm that a connection can be created. A connection being available is one thing. The complete reporting experience working as expected is another.

What I now look at when a chart does not behave as expected

These experiences have changed how I approach troubleshooting in SAC.

Earlier in the process, it is tempting to start with the widget itself. Change the measure, change the aggregation, adjust the filter, or try a different chart. Sometimes that is exactly where the problem is.

But I find it more useful to work backwards from the result.

If a KPI is showing zero, I want to know whether the analytical model also returns zero.

If a filter produces an unexpected result, I want to know whether the model contains the necessary dimension and whether the filter is reaching the intended widgets.

If a story works but a Work Zone tile fails, I want to understand how that tile retrieves the data and whether the connection scenario is supported.

The troubleshooting path depends on the symptom, but the underlying approach is the same.

Start with what the user sees. Identify the layer responsible for producing that result. Then verify the assumptions at that layer before changing anything. That approach helps distinguish between a data problem, a modeling problem, a story configuration problem, and a platform integration problem.

It also avoids a common trap in analytics development: changing something that appears related to the symptom without establishing that it caused the issue.

The final mile is where the business judges the entire landscape

Looking back at the three stages of this analytics journey, I see them as closely connected.

In the first stage, we worked on understanding and translating the existing BW reporting logic.

In the second, we dealt with the challenges of bringing S/4HANA data into Datasphere and making sure it was technically, structurally, and semantically suitable for reporting.

In the final stage, we had to turn those models into an analytical experience that the business could use and trust.

Each stage has its own problems, but the final stage brings the earlier decisions together. 
A beautifully designed SAC story cannot compensate for incorrect business logic. 
A correct Datasphere model does not guarantee that every filter, widget, or integration will behave as expected.

And a successful connection does not, by itself, guarantee a successful reporting experience.

For me, this is the part of analytics development that is easy to underestimate. The final charts are visible, so they naturally receive a lot of attention. But what makes those charts trustworthy is everything behind them, together with the decisions made when connecting the model to the user experience.

The goal is not simply to get data onto a screen.

It is to make sure the number on that screen means what the business thinks it means, and that users can access it in the context where they need it.

That is when the analytics landscape starts delivering its real value.

Because ultimately, the model is the foundation, the chart is the interface, and the business decision is the outcome.

entry.title: How do you handle missing exchange rates without compromising financial reporting?
entry.content:
Hi everyone,

I've been thinking about a scenario that can easily become a data-quality issue in SAP Finance reporting.

Imagine we're building a Finance analytical model in SAP Datasphere. We have transaction amounts in different currencies, and we need to convert them into a common reporting currency using exchange rates from TCURR.

Now consider this scenario:

  • A transaction is posted on 15 October in USD.

  • The reporting currency is EUR.

  • The model looks for the applicable USD-to-EUR exchange rate for that date.

  • The required rate isn't available in the exchange-rate data.

What should happen next?

We could leave the converted amount empty, flag the transaction for investigation, or use the most recent available rate. Each approach has different implications for reporting accuracy.

Using the previous available rate might seem practical, but it could also produce a misleading financial figure if the business expects the rate valid for the transaction date.

I'm curious how others handle this in SAP Datasphere and S/4HANA Finance implementations.

  1. Do you fail validation when the required exchange rate is missing, or allow the model to continue with a flagged amount?

  2. If you use the previous available rate, how do you validate it and prevent an outdated rate from being used indefinitely?

  3. Where do you implement this logic: during data preparation, in the graphical view, or in the analytical model?

  4. How do you distinguish a genuinely missing rate from a rate that exists under a different exchange-rate type or quotation convention?

I'd particularly like to hear about approaches that preserve financial accuracy while keeping reporting models maintainable.

Thanks!

entry.title: Model company for SAP cloud solutions for Architects: From Target Architecture to an Executable Base
entry.content:
Part 2 of a blog series on model company for SAP cloud solutions

Introduction

 

Every architect knows the moment: the target architecture is documented in capability maps, process models and solution designs, but the next question is how to turn that intent into decisions the implementation team can validate and deliver.

This is my second post in the model company for SAP cloud solutions series. The first post introduced the overall proposition and the move toward Fit-to-Standard. Here, the focus is on the decisions enterprise and solution architects need to make.

Model company provides a pre-configured, executable SAP S/4HANA reference baseline with available industry and line-of-business content. It does not define every customer’s target architecture. Instead, it gives architects a working reference against which to assess capability coverage, question assumptions and identify the design decisions that remain.

Figure 1: From architectural intent to an executable reference. Model company provides a baseline for validation, not a finished customer architecture.

The Architect’s Challenge: From Design to Executable Reality

 

Target architectures describe what an organization wants to achieve; implementation teams must determine how that intent can be realized in a configured solution. The handover between the two often exposes uncertainties: Is a process already supported by standard SAP functionality? Which assumptions need testing? What requires integration, configuration or an extension?

Model company helps bridge this gap by making relevant standard processes and industry content tangible. Architects can explore and demonstrate a working reference rather than relying exclusively on diagrams or descriptions. The reference does not remove the need for discovery or customer-specific validation; it makes those activities more focused.

This supports a change in mindset, from Fit-to-Gap (“how do we reproduce what we do today?”) to Fit-to-Standard (“can the standard support the intended outcome, and where is differentiation genuinely necessary?”). The question is not whether the standard is always sufficient, but how to make deviations evidence-based architectural decisions.

Figure 2: Changing the conversation: assess business outcomes against the standard before specifying deviations.

An Architect’s Workflow: A Retail Example

 

Consider an illustrative retail transformation. The target architecture calls for improved inventory visibility, a consistent order-fulfillment process and reliable financial integration. Rather than treating every existing customization as a requirement, the architecture team can use the relevant model company reference to structure its assessment.

  • Identify the capabilities: map the target business outcomes to the processes and application responsibilities that must support them.
  • Explore the baseline: examine available retail processes and associated artifacts in the model company system. Confirm which scope and release are available.
  • Validate assumptions: demonstrate representative flows with sample data; compare the standard with key business scenarios and record the functional or non-functional questions still open.
  • Make design choices: Distinguish standard coverage from required configuration, interfaces, data work, and genuinely differentiating extensions. For each proposed deviation, document its justification, expected business value, and implications for complexity, cost, and long-term maintainability.
  • Carry decisions into delivery: use relevant process models, scope artifacts and governance tools to connect decisions to implementation requirements, testing and change control.

The result is not an automatically generated target architecture. It is a better-evidenced design: the team knows what it has validated, where uncertainty remains and which decisions require architectural ownership.

 

How It Helps Enterprise Architects

 

Enterprise architects connect strategy, business capabilities and the target operating model with the application landscape.

Model company can help them:

  • Assess capability realization in a running reference and distinguish demonstrated scope from capabilities that still require further design.
  • Relate reference business architecture and process models to the actual standard processes delivered in the relevant industry or line of business.
  • Create a shared starting point for business stakeholders, enterprise architecture and delivery teams, reducing misunderstandings about what “standard” means.
  • Inform roadmap and scoping decisions by checking current content availability, release coverage and relevant prerequisites rather than assuming that every planned capability is already delivered.

How It Helps Solution Architects

 

Solution architects translate the target into process, data, application, integration and extension decisions. Against a pre-configured reference, they can:

  • Explore representative end-to-end processes instead of starting each discussion from an unconfigured system.
  • Inspect sample master and transactional data and identify interfaces or integration requirements; a visible integration point does not necessarily mean that a connected external system has been delivered.
  • Evaluate standard functionality first, then select suitable clean-core-aligned extensibility options based on the requirement and deployment environment.
  • Use process and delivery artifacts to support documented scope, requirements and testing decisions, with traceability governed through the chosen project toolchain.

Connecting Architecture to the Delivery Toolchain

 

SAP LeanIX supports enterprise architecture and application landscape decisions; SAP Signavio provides a comprehensive process intelligence and transformation suite for process-modeling and business transformation; and SAP Cloud ALM is a full lifecycle application management platform, covering implementation governance, operations monitoring, and continuous improvement.

For transformation initiatives, it delivers end-to-end project management, structured requirements handling, and test governance, making it the central control point for managing SAP solution deployments.

Model company contributes a working reference and associated artifacts that can be used alongside these tools.

The precise artifacts available depend on the selected model company scope and release. Process models, documentation, test assets and sample data can support design and Fit-to-Standard workshops, but architects should verify what is included and how it can be accessed or imported. Viewing process content and importing or synchronizing it into a customer workspace may have different licensing and authorization requirements.

Importantly, traceability is not automatic. Connecting process models, scope, requirements and test evidence requires tool configuration, appropriate entitlements, disciplined ownership and project governance. SAP Signavio, SAP Cloud ALM synchronization, for example, has defined setup and license prerequisites.

 

Where It Fits in SAP Activate

 

Model company brings its most immediate value to early validation and Fit-to-Standard work, particularly during Explore. Its reference content and artifacts may also inform later implementation phases.

The model company system remains a reference/sandbox environment: it is not the productive customer solution and should not be described as directly deploying into production.

  • Discover and Prepare: use the available baseline to illustrate potential scope, challenge target-state assumptions and prepare more focused architectural discussions.
  • Explore (Fit-to-Standard): run relevant scenarios against the standard, assess business fit, identify genuine deltas and agree which requirements need additional design.
  • Realize: use validated decisions and applicable reference artifacts to guide implementation; govern architecture conformance, interfaces, extensions and test coverage in the customer project.
  • Deploy: confirm that the implemented productive solution meets the approved architecture, security, integration and operational criteria. This is a customer-project responsibility, not a deployment of the model company sandbox.
  • Run: maintain architectural guardrails, assess changing needs against standard capabilities, and govern extensions and process evolution over time.

The continuous thread is controlled decision-making: from intended business capability, through process validation and design, to implementation evidence. The architecture team can establish traceability across that chain but must actively maintain it.

Figure 3: Model company in SAP Activate. Explore is the primary direct validation point; later phases benefit from the reference and decisions carried forward.

Keeping the Core Clean: Extensibility Governance

 

Clean core is an architectural discipline, not a property that eliminates governance. It aims to keep the SAP core close to standard, use appropriate extension mechanisms and released interfaces, and support maintainability and future upgrades. Model company, built on SAP Best Practices that bring standard Line of Business business processes and aligned with clean-core principles, gives architects a useful starting reference, not an unconditional guarantee of customer-specific compliance or upgrade safety.

  • Challenge proposed deviations: demonstrate what standard content already covers before agreeing to custom build; record business rationale and architectural consequences for justified gaps.
  • Choose the right extension pattern: consider approved key-user, developer/on-stack and side-by-side extensibility, including SAP BTP where appropriate. The right choice depends on requirements, release and deployment model; “side-by-side” is not the answer to every extension.
  • Govern integration explicitly: design interfaces around applicable released APIs and supported integration patterns, while validating external systems, security, performance and data responsibilities.
  • Keep decisions traceable: link requirements, architectural decisions, process changes and tests within the project’s governed toolchain, rather than assuming the reference environment does this automatically.

By reducing unnecessary custom code and providing a clean-core-aligned reference, model company simplifies architectural decision-making and lifecycle management, while enabling architects to focus their assessments on customer-specific requirements, integrations, and extensions.

 

What Architects Still Need to Validate

 

A reference baseline is most useful when its boundaries are clear.

Architects must still confirm:

  • Industry and country coverage
  • Business-process fit
  • The customer’s application and integration landscape
  • Data migration and ownership
  • Non-functional requirements
  • Security and regulatory obligations
  • Extension design
  • Licensing or technical prerequisites for connected tools.

The strongest use of model company is therefore not to declare the architecture complete. It is to expose and resolve architectural questions earlier, while keeping legitimate differentiation visible and controlled.

 

From Clean Core to Validated AI Capabilities

 

Clean-core principles, standardized processes, and governed data provide a strong foundation for sustainable AI adoption. Model company for SAP cloud solutions builds on this foundation, with Joule already activated and successfully tested in selected model company environments. In addition, AI use cases have been tested and validated and are ready for inclusion, progressively extending the portfolio’s ability to demonstrate AI-enabled business processes.

For architects, this creates an opportunity to move beyond conceptual AI discussions and explore how intelligent capabilities can be incorporated into business processes and solution architectures. These validated scenarios provide tangible reference points for assessing architectural dependencies, integration requirements, and the potential role of AI within a customer’s target landscape.

AI enablement is progressing across the model company portfolio, with capabilities and availability varying by industry and line of business. Their adoption within a customer environment remains subject to scenario availability, release compatibility, licensing and entitlements, technical prerequisites, and applicable AI consumption arrangements.

By combining a clean-core-aligned baseline with activated Joule capabilities and validated AI use cases, model company helps architects bridge the gap between AI strategy and practical enablement.

 

Conclusion: A Better Starting Point for Architectural Decisions

 

Model company changes the starting point, not the architect’s responsibility. Instead of working only from abstract models or a blank configuration, teams can examine a tangible, SAP-delivered baseline and use it to validate assumptions, challenge unnecessary complexity and make more informed Fit-to-Standard decisions.

Whether your role is enterprise architecture or solution architecture, the benefit is a clearer distinction between what the reference already demonstrates, what the customer genuinely needs and what must still be designed and governed.

Start with one critical capability from your target architecture. Explore the model company content available for the relevant industry, test the associated process assumptions and document where the standard fits or where further decisions are needed.

  • Designing integrations
